11:15.topic: What college coaches evaluate in a catcher
11:15.alt_text: A young baseball catcher in full gear crouches behind the plate on a sunny field, ready for the pitch.
11:15.headline: Catchers: more than a pop time
11:15.caption:
Pop time gets the headlines. Coaches watch everything that happens before and after the throw.

If your son catches, here's what college staffs tend to evaluate:

⚾ Receiving. Does he catch the low strike quietly and give the umpire a clean look?
⚾ Blocking. Can he keep balls in the dirt in front of him with runners on?
⚾ Throwing. Pop time is the glove-to-glove time on a throw to second. Accuracy counts as much as speed.
⚾ Running the game. How he works with pitchers, sets up hitters and talks to the infield.
⚾ The bat. A catcher who can hit adds a lot of value to a lineup.

Coaches often trust a catcher who receives and blocks well over one with a big arm and stiff hands.

15:30.topic: What a pitcher should track beyond velocity
15:30.concept: Clean 'pitching log' notebook layout, cream paper texture on navy, green handwritten-style checkmarks; one metric per slide. Slide 1 hook: 'Velo gets the attention. These get him innings.' Slides 2-4: Strikes / Second pitch / Holding stuff late. Slide 5 takeaway: 'Track it all spring. Save this.'
15:30.headline: Velo gets the attention. These get him innings.
15:30.caption:
Velocity gets the attention. Strikes get him innings.

If your son pitches, radar readings are only part of what college coaches look at. A few things worth tracking all spring:

⚾ Strike rate. How often is he in the zone, especially on the first pitch?
⚾ A second pitch he trusts. Can he throw it for a strike when he's behind in the count?
⚾ Holding his stuff. Does his command stay sharp in the fourth and fifth innings?
⚾ Walks. Free passes add up fast, and coaches notice.

A simple notebook after every outing tells a clearer story than one radar reading at a showcase.

19:30.topic: Playing time vs a bigger-name program
19:30.overlay: Small text overlay top-left: 'Would you rather...' with two lines 'A: Play as a freshman' / 'B: Bigger-name program'
19:30.alt_text: Two baseball players in uniform walk onto the field together before a game.
19:30.headline: Play now or bigger name?
19:30.caption:
Two offers on the table. Which way would your family lean?

A. A smaller program where he's likely to compete for innings or at-bats as a freshman.
B. A bigger-name program where he may wait a year or two to see the field.

There's no wrong answer. Some players grow by competing every day against older teammates. Others need game reps to keep developing. Academics, cost, coaching staff and how he handles a backup role all belong in the conversation.

Best fit beats biggest name, but fit means something different for every player.

Reply A or B and tell us why. 👇 Send this to a baseball parent who's been there.
